title: Privacy program governance, accountable owner, inventory and notice
status_rationale: No adopted privacy policy, privacy notice, record of processing or appointed privacy owner was located. The Unbound control matrix proposes a Privacy Officer role (UNB-CTRL-085..087) with status Designed and no operating evidence.
target_answer: Echelon operates a written privacy program owned by a named Privacy Officer who reports to the managing member at least quarterly. A machine-readable record of processing is generated from the Strata schema catalog, in which every column carries a data category and purpose tag, so the inventory cannot drift from the deployed schema. The platform privacy notice is versioned in Praxis-governed records, and privacy training is role-based and tracked. Program effectiveness is examined in a SOC 2 Type II report that includes the Privacy or Confidentiality criteria once the service is in production.
current_practice: Unknown; no evidence located of a privacy policy, notice, inventory, training or named owner.
intended_practice: Adopt a privacy program before the first customer contract; derive the processing inventory from schema metadata; scope Privacy criteria into the first SOC 2 examination if customers require it.
provable: Nothing. No program documents exist to show.
customer_statement: Echelon has not yet established a formal privacy program, privacy notice or named privacy officer. We can share the proposed design for review and will not represent it as operating.
external_assurance: None. No SOC 2 report, ISO certification, privacy assessment or other independent assurance exists for any Echelon service as of 2026-11-25.
owner: Managing member (interim) until a Privacy Officer is appointed
residual_risks: A single-founder organization cannot separate program ownership from engineering, which weakens independent challenge.
open_questions: Who will hold the Privacy Officer role, and will it be an employee, the founder, or a fractional external provider?
Will the first SOC 2 examination include the Privacy or Confidentiality criteria, and which do target customers require?

title: Processing role (processor, service provider) and applicability of CCPA/CPRA and state privacy laws
status_rationale: Unbound requirements treat the sponsor as the authority over fund data (CNV-PAY-001 treats Unbound as a third-party service provider for payments) and require per-partner DPAs (UNB-TEN-008). No legal analysis of Echelon's role under CCPA or other state laws exists.
target_answer: For the Unbound service Echelon acts only as a processor, service provider or contractor on the sponsor's documented instructions. Echelon's own uses are limited to an enumerated list (security, fraud prevention, debugging, service improvement without cross-customer data combination) that the contract names. The DPA carries the CCPA service-provider terms where the customer is a covered business, and the equivalent processor terms required by state laws that cover nonprofits (for example Colorado and Oregon). Role determinations per data flow are recorded and reviewed by counsel.
current_practice: Not established. No DPA template, role analysis or counsel opinion exists.
intended_practice: Commission a counsel memo on Echelon's role by customer type (nonprofit sponsor, bank, RIA, broker-dealer, for-profit partner) and adopt a DPA that satisfies the strictest applicable regime.
provable: Nothing operational. Only requirement text in the Unbound baseline (unbound@9b38de47) can be shown, and it proves intent, not operation.
customer_statement: Unbound is not yet in production. Its requirements specify that the sponsor controls fund data and that Echelon processes it on the sponsor's behalf. Echelon has not yet completed a legal analysis of its role under specific state privacy laws. This is a design commitment, not an operating control, and has not been independently verified.
external_assurance: None. No SOC 2 report, ISO certification, privacy assessment or other independent assurance exists for any Echelon service as of 2026-11-25.
open_questions: Most DAF sponsors are nonprofit public charities that fall outside the CCPA definition of 'business'. Does Echelon have any CCPA service-provider obligation when its customer is not a CCPA business, and does that change for for-profit partner programs?
Which state comprehensive privacy laws cover nonprofit controllers that would be Echelon customers, and do any of their processor obligations apply to Echelon directly?
Where a state law exempts GLBA-covered financial institutions or GLBA-covered data, does that exemption reach donor data held for a nonprofit sponsor?

challenge.customer_intent: Customer wants assurance that the vendor will not become an independent controller of donor data.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Vendor uses donor data for its own purposes, or the customer cannot meet its own state-law processor-contract obligations.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Contract role labels are effective only to the extent the vendor's systems actually prevent unlisted uses; a label alone is not a control.
challenge.legally_required: Depends on customer type. Required where the customer is a CCPA business or a controller under a state law that covers nonprofits; uncertain for nonprofit sponsors in states that exempt them.
challenge.contractually_required: Commonly required by bank, RIA and enterprise customers regardless of statutory applicability.
challenge.historical_convention: Processor and service-provider terms are standard SaaS practice inherited from GDPR Article 28.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Purpose limitation can be partly enforced by architecture: no analytics pipeline exists that can read tenant data across tenants, and Echelon-internal uses run through declared, audited interfaces.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Authorization policy can deny any Echelon-internal principal access to tenant data except through declared purposes, with every access logged.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Access logs by purpose can be exported to the customer continuously.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Purpose-bound access enforced in the authorization layer plus customer-visible access logs, alongside contract terms.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Yes, by negative tests and access-log review, once built.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Contract terms will still be required; the architectural control is additive.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: Any internal pipeline or AI agent that bypasses the authorization layer invalidates the purpose-bound claim.
challenge.alternative_risks: Over-restriction could block legitimate security and support access during incidents.
supporting_arguments: Makes the processor claim checkable rather than asserted.
Satisfies multiple state regimes with one mechanism.
opposing_arguments: Customers and counsel will still insist on contract terms; architecture does not substitute.
Applicability analysis for nonprofit customers is unsettled, so overcommitting to statutory language could create obligations not otherwise owed.

title: GLBA, Regulation P, Safeguards Rule and Regulation S-P obligations flowing to Echelon
status_rationale: Unbound research records that GLBA applicability to a nonprofit sponsor is doubtful and that a for-profit vendor is a GLBA financial institution only if its own activities are financial (unbound@9b38de47:requirements/discovery/2026-11-23-cross-industry/industry/grt.md). No contractual safeguards terms or incident-notification procedure exist.
target_answer: Echelon treats donor financial data as if it were nonpublic personal information regardless of the unsettled GLBA status of a particular sponsor, so one control set serves banks, RIAs, broker-dealers and nonprofit sponsors. It accepts service-provider safeguards terms that bank customers need under the Interagency Guidelines, notifies covered institutions under amended Regulation S-P of a breach of customer information no later than 72 hours after becoming aware of it, limits reuse and redisclosure of NPI to the purposes for which it was received, and maintains a written information security program meeting the FTC Safeguards Rule elements whether or not Echelon is itself determined to be a financial institution.
current_practice: Not established. GLBA status of Echelon and of DAF sponsors is unresolved.
intended_practice: Obtain counsel analysis per customer type; adopt the Safeguards Rule element set as the internal baseline; build a 72-hour customer notification runbook.
provable: Nothing operational. Only requirement text in the Unbound baseline (unbound@9b38de47) can be shown, and it proves intent, not operation.
customer_statement: Echelon has not determined whether it or its DAF sponsor customers are financial institutions under GLBA. Unbound is designed to treat donor financial data with safeguards suitable for regulated financial institutions, and Echelon intends to accept service-provider terms that bank and SEC-registered customers require. No such program operates today.
external_assurance: None. No SOC 2 report, ISO certification, privacy assessment or other independent assurance exists for any Echelon service as of 2026-11-25.
open_questions: Is a nonprofit DAF sponsor a 'financial institution' under GLBA, and if not, does any GLBA obligation reach Echelon through it? This is not settled and must not be resolved by assumption.
Does Echelon's own activity (payment preparation as a Nacha TPSP, account servicing) make it a financial institution under the FTC Safeguards Rule definitions?
If Echelon is a financial institution under the Safeguards Rule, does the FTC notification requirement for security events affecting 500 or more consumers apply to it directly?

title: Data processing agreement terms: subprocessors, instructions, audit and flow-down
status_rationale: UNB-TEN-008 requires support for per-partner data processing agreements. No DPA template, subprocessor list or notification mechanism exists.
target_answer: Echelon offers a standard DPA before contract that covers processing on documented instructions, confidentiality, security measures, subprocessor authorization with advance notice and a right to object, assistance with rights requests and assessments, breach notification, return and deletion at end of service, and audit rights satisfied first by independent reports and, where required, by on-site or remote audit. A machine-readable subprocessor register (including AI model providers) is published with change history, and every subprocessor contract carries equivalent obligations.
current_practice: Not established. No DPA, subprocessor register or flow-down terms exist.
intended_practice: Draft a DPA meeting GDPR Article 28 and CCPA service-provider requirements as the strictest common denominator; publish a versioned subprocessor register.
provable: Nothing operational. Only requirement text in the Unbound baseline (unbound@9b38de47) can be shown, and it proves intent, not operation.
customer_statement: Echelon does not yet have a standard DPA or subprocessor list. Unbound's design requires per-sponsor processing agreements, and Echelon intends to offer a DPA with subprocessor notice, audit and flow-down terms before any production contract.
external_assurance: None. No SOC 2 report, ISO certification, privacy assessment or other independent assurance exists for any Echelon service as of 2026-11-25.
open_questions: Which AI model providers will be subprocessors, and do their terms permit equivalent flow-down obligations, including no training on customer data?

title: Data subject rights handling and the append-only record conflict
status_rationale: UNB-DATA-007, UNB-IMM-008, SOC2-032 and UNB-GAP-021 require rights handling through reviewed architecture without false deletion promises; SOC-T15 is a proposed test. Nothing is built.
target_answer: Rights requests reach the sponsor, which decides; Echelon provides tooling that locates every record about a person across funds, successor and joint-advisor relationships, events, documents, logs and exports, and executes the decision within contractual timelines. Deletion is fulfilled by erasing the person's entry in a segregated encrypted identity vault (cryptographic erasure of the per-person key) while legally required financial records remain with pseudonymous references, and the customer receives a statement of exactly what was erased and what was retained and why. Requests reaching Echelon directly are forwarded to the sponsor within two business days.
intended_practice: Build identity vault and per-person key design (UNB-DATA-007) before first production data; define rights workflow with sponsor decision step.
provable: Nothing operational. Only requirement text in the Unbound baseline (unbound@9b38de47) can be shown, and it proves intent, not operation.
customer_statement: Unbound is not yet in production. Its requirements specify that privacy rights requests be handled through a reviewed architecture, with personal data kept out of immutable records where possible, and that Echelon not promise deletion of records it must retain. This is a design commitment, not an operating control, and has not been independently verified.
external_assurance: None. No SOC 2 report, ISO certification, privacy assessment or other independent assurance exists for any Echelon service as of 2026-11-25.
residual_risks: Cryptographic erasure does not remove plaintext already copied to backups, logs, exports or third parties (UNB-IMM-008).
open_questions: Which donor rights apply at all when the sponsor is a nonprofit outside CCPA and the donor's state law exempts nonprofits or GLBA data?
Can a donor's request to delete be honored for a fund the sponsor legally owns, given that the donor relinquished control of contributed assets?

challenge.customer_intent: Customer wants to honor donor rights without breaking record-keeping duties or ledger integrity.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Either a donor's lawful deletion right is refused because of the architecture, or deletion destroys records the sponsor must keep.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Conventional row deletion in a mutable database is simple but conflicts with append-only ledgers and leaves copies in backups and logs.
challenge.legally_required: Deletion rights exist only where an applicable law grants them; many nonprofit sponsors may be outside comprehensive state laws, and financial record retention exceptions are common.
challenge.historical_convention: Mutable CRUD systems answered deletion by deleting rows.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Keeping personal identifiers out of immutable payloads and in a keyed vault eliminates most of the conflict by construction.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Key destruction is a single auditable operation; projections rebuilt from events lose access automatically.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Vault key inventory and erasure events can be reported continuously.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Identity vault with per-person keys plus pseudonymous ledger references.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Partly: key destruction is verifiable; absence of plaintext elsewhere requires scanning and design review.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Regulators and counsel accept cryptographic erasure in some contexts; acceptance for this use is not established.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: Plaintext identifiers in event payloads, free-text notes, documents, logs or exports defeat the design.
challenge.conventional_cost: Low to build, high to defend when it conflicts with an append-only ledger.
challenge.alternative_cost: High: vault, key management, scanning and projection rebuild design.
challenge.alternative_risks: Key management failure could make legitimately retained records unreadable.
supporting_arguments: Resolves the append-only versus deletion conflict structurally.
Gives a precise, auditable account of what was erased.
opposing_arguments: Cryptographic erasure is not universally accepted as deletion.
Free-text fields and documents make complete separation hard.
Adds operational risk of accidental key loss.

title: No sale, sharing, advertising use or monetization of customer data
status_rationale: SOC2-028 and UNB-TEN-007 constrain permitted use and cross-tenant flows; no explicit no-sale commitment exists in a contract because no contract exists.
target_answer: Echelon does not sell or share customer personal data, does not use it for targeted or cross-context behavioral advertising, receives no third-party compensation tied to donor data, and does not create cross-customer benchmarks or data products from customer data. Any aggregate statistics are produced only with written sponsor opt-in and a published de-identification method. The platform has no advertising or data-broker integrations, which is checkable from the egress allowlist and subprocessor register.
current_practice: Not established. No data monetization exists because no service operates.
intended_practice: Commit in contract and design; enforce cross-tenant prohibitions under UNB-TEN-007.
provable: Nothing operational. Only requirement text in the Unbound baseline (unbound@9b38de47) can be shown, and it proves intent, not operation.
customer_statement: Echelon's intended position is that it will not sell, share or monetize customer data or use it for advertising. Unbound is not in production and this commitment is not yet in a signed contract.
external_assurance: None. No SOC 2 report, ISO certification, privacy assessment or other independent assurance exists for any Echelon service as of 2026-11-25.
open_questions: Will Echelon want aggregate, cross-sponsor analytics (for example charity intelligence) in future, and if so under what consent model?

challenge.customer_intent: Customer wants assurance that donor data is not a revenue source for the vendor.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Donor data monetized or leaked to marketers, damaging donor trust and the sponsor's reputation.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: A contractual promise is effective only if breaches would be detected; customers rarely can detect them.
challenge.legally_required: Required as service-provider terms where CCPA or similar laws apply; otherwise contractual.
challenge.contractually_required: Common in enterprise and financial DPAs.
challenge.historical_convention: Data brokerage by SaaS vendors made this a standard ask.
challenge.architectural_elimination: No advertising SDKs, data-broker connectors or cross-tenant analytics stores exist in the architecture.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Egress allowlist bound to the published subprocessor register blocks unlisted recipients.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Egress configuration and subprocessor register are publishable as continuous evidence.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Contract promise plus verifiable absence of monetization paths.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Yes, by configuration review and egress logs.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Likely; it supplements rather than replaces the contract.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: Any future product that uses cross-customer data invalidates the claim unless separately consented.
challenge.alternative_risks: Egress restrictions may hinder support tooling.
supporting_arguments: Turns a promise into a checkable configuration.
opposing_arguments: Customers cannot independently observe egress without an audit.
Future business pressure to monetize aggregate data is not constrained by architecture alone.

title: Data location, residency and international transfers
status_rationale: CNV-ARC-001 specifies one managed PostgreSQL cluster; UNB-TEN-008 requires per-partner residency where applicable. No hosting provider or region has been selected; no transfer mechanism exists.
target_answer: All Unbound production data, backups and AI inference run in United States regions of named providers, and support or engineering access, including by AI agents, originates from approved US locations and is logged with origin. A residency commitment is enforced by infrastructure policy that rejects resources outside approved regions. Where personal data of EU or UK residents is processed (for example donors living abroad or foreign grantee signatories), Echelon offers the 2021 SCCs (Module 2 or 3) and the UK addendum, with a transfer impact assessment; Echelon does not currently claim Data Privacy Framework certification.
current_practice: Not established. No hosting provider, region or transfer mechanism has been selected.
intended_practice: Select US regions; encode region restrictions as deploy-time policy; decide whether DPF certification is worth its cost given expected EU data volume.
provable: Nothing operational. Only requirement text in the Unbound baseline (unbound@9b38de47) can be shown, and it proves intent, not operation.
customer_statement: Echelon intends to host Unbound in the United States and has not yet selected a provider or region. Echelon is not certified under the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework.
external_assurance: None. No SOC 2 report, ISO certification, privacy assessment or other independent assurance exists for any Echelon service as of 2026-11-25.
open_questions: Will any foreign personnel, contractors or AI model provider endpoints access production data?
Does the US Department of Justice rule restricting bulk sensitive personal data transfers to countries of concern apply to any planned data flow (source not seeded)?

title: Privacy by design, privacy impact assessment and production data in development
status_rationale: SOC2-030 requires a security and privacy design review before new data categories, external APIs, autonomous permissions or financial workflows. No review has been performed because nothing is built.
target_answer: Every change that introduces a data category, external API, AI agent permission or financial workflow requires a recorded privacy impact assessment linked to the change in Praxis; the release gate blocks merges that touch tagged schema elements without a linked assessment. Defaults favor privacy: donor names hidden from grantees unless chosen, minimal fields visible to charities and partners. Production personal data is never used in development or by AI coding agents; synthetic data is generated from schema definitions.
intended_practice: Define the PIA template and gate; build synthetic data generation from schema.
provable: Nothing operational. Only requirement text in the Unbound baseline (unbound@9b38de47) can be shown, and it proves intent, not operation.
customer_statement: Unbound is not yet in production. Its requirements specify a privacy and security design review before introducing new data categories, external APIs, autonomous permissions or financial workflows. This is a design commitment, not an operating control, and has not been independently verified.
external_assurance: None. No SOC 2 report, ISO certification, privacy assessment or other independent assurance exists for any Echelon service as of 2026-11-25.
open_questions: Can Praxis link a change record to a PIA record and expose that link to a CI gate today, or does this need new Praxis capability?

title: Cookies, tracking technologies and third-party scripts in donor portals
status_rationale: Unbound UI is intended to use Limen (browser boundary, only serializable data crosses) and Forma (zero-runtime CSS) per UNB-TEC-002. No portal exists and no tracking decision is recorded.
target_answer: Donor, advisor and charity portals load no third-party scripts, advertising pixels, session replay or cross-site trackers. Only strictly necessary first-party cookies for authentication and security are set, so no consent banner is needed in most US states; any optional first-party analytics is aggregate, cookieless and server-side. Content Security Policy forbids third-party script origins, and a CI check fails the build when one is introduced. Identifiers never appear in URLs.
intended_practice: Adopt a no-third-party-script rule enforced by CSP and CI; document the cookie inventory.
provable: Nothing operational. Only requirement text in the Unbound baseline (unbound@9b38de47) can be shown, and it proves intent, not operation.
customer_statement: Echelon intends donor portals to run without third-party tracking scripts. No portal is in production.
external_assurance: None. No SOC 2 report, ISO certification, privacy assessment or other independent assurance exists for any Echelon service as of 2026-11-25.
open_questions: Will sponsors in white-label programs demand their own analytics tags on donor pages, and will Echelon refuse?

challenge.customer_intent: Customer wants donor browsing and giving activity kept away from ad networks.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Pixels transmit donor activity, including grants to religious or political causes, to third parties; tracking litigation risk.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Consent banners and cookie policies are weak: they shift responsibility to the donor and are routinely misconfigured.
challenge.legally_required: Consent or opt-out obligations depend on state law and whether tracking occurs; eliminating tracking removes most obligations.
challenge.contractually_required: Customers commonly ask for a cookie inventory.
challenge.historical_convention: Consumer web practice normalized third-party analytics on authenticated pages.
challenge.architectural_elimination: No third-party scripts at all; CSP forbids external script origins.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: CI check on CSP and asset origins; runtime CSP violation reports.
challenge.continuous_evidence: CSP header and violation report stream are continuous evidence.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Eliminate tracking rather than manage consent for it.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Yes, by inspecting response headers and page loads.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Likely for financial customers; sponsor marketing teams may object.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: Any sponsor-requested tag or embedded third-party widget (for example chat or video) breaks the guarantee.
challenge.conventional_cost: Medium: consent management platform and cookie audits.
challenge.alternative_risks: Loss of marketing analytics that sponsors may value.
supporting_arguments: Removes a whole class of disclosure and litigation risk.
opposing_arguments: Sponsors may insist on their own analytics.
Some support and accessibility tools are delivered as third-party scripts.

title: Children's and minors' data
status_rationale: Unbound supports successors and next-generation advisors (UNB-SUCC-001, UNB-GAP-015) but no requirement addresses minors' data or age handling.
target_answer: The service is not directed to children and does not permit accounts for users under 18. Minors named as successors or beneficiaries are recorded with the minimum data needed (name and relationship), visible only to the sponsor and the advising donor, and cannot log in until they reach majority and are verified. Any future youth philanthropy feature requires a PIA and counsel review against COPPA and state minors' privacy laws before design.
current_practice: Unknown; no requirement or design decision located.
intended_practice: Add an explicit requirement for minors in succession records; decide whether any youth feature is in scope.
customer_statement: Echelon has not yet defined how minors' data is handled in Unbound. The service is not intended for use by children.
external_assurance: None. No SOC 2 report, ISO certification, privacy assessment or other independent assurance exists for any Echelon service as of 2026-11-25.
open_questions: Will Unbound ever support custodial or youth giving accounts? If so COPPA and state minors' laws need analysis; no COPPA source is seeded.

title: Use of customer data for AI training, model providers and AI agent access
status_rationale: SOC2-028 requires permitted AI use to be reflected in access, storage, retrieval and exports; UNB-CTL-001 bars probabilistic outputs from clearing controls or moving money; the business plan section 10.04 names training rights as a topic but states no concrete position (echelon-organization-administration@2763e576:business-plan/10-technology-data-and-ai/10.04-client-data-and-training-rights.md).
target_answer: Echelon does not use customer data to train, fine-tune or evaluate models, and contracts with model providers prohibit training on and retention of prompts and outputs beyond the minimum needed for abuse monitoring, with zero-retention options used where available. AI agents performing engineering and operations work have no standing access to production customer data; any access is break-glass, purpose-declared, scoped to one tenant and logged. Customers can disable all AI processing of their tenant's data, which is enforced in the authorization layer rather than by configuration of individual features.
current_practice: Not established. No model provider contracts, AI feature or tenant AI switch exists. Echelon's engineering work uses AI agents on source code, not on customer data, since no customer data exists.
intended_practice: Write the no-training commitment into the DPA; select model providers with contractual no-training and limited retention; implement tenant AI opt-out in authorization.
provable: Nothing operational. Only requirement text in the Unbound baseline (unbound@9b38de47) can be shown, and it proves intent, not operation.
customer_statement: Echelon's intended position is that customer data is not used to train AI models and that AI agents do not have standing access to production customer data. No AI feature processes customer data today because Unbound is not in production.
external_assurance: None. No SOC 2 report, ISO certification, privacy assessment or other independent assurance exists for any Echelon service as of 2026-11-25.
residual_risks: Model provider retention for abuse monitoring is governed by provider terms Echelon does not control.
open_questions: Business plan 10.04 does not state Echelon's actual position on training rights; the owner needs to decide it explicitly.
Which model providers and endpoints will be used, and what are their current retention and training terms?

challenge.customer_intent: Customer wants assurance that donor data will not be absorbed into models that serve others or leak through outputs.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Donor data memorized in a model, disclosed via outputs, or used to benefit competitors.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Contractual no-training promises are hard for customers to verify.
challenge.legally_required: No general statute prohibits training on processor data, but processor-purpose limits under privacy laws and DPAs restrict it where they apply.
challenge.contractually_required: Increasingly standard in enterprise DPAs and AI addenda.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Echelon has no training pipeline; the absence of any training infrastructure can be shown.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Tenant AI switch enforced in authorization; model calls route through one gateway that tags tenant and checks the switch.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Gateway logs of every model call with tenant, purpose and provider are continuous evidence.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Single model gateway with per-call tenant tagging, provider allowlist and opt-out enforcement.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Yes, by gateway logs and negative tests.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Likely; customers still want the contractual commitment.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: Direct model calls that bypass the gateway, or provider terms that change, invalidate the claim.
challenge.alternative_risks: Gateway is a single point of failure for AI features.
supporting_arguments: Same gateway supports provider retention checks.
opposing_arguments: Gateway logs themselves may contain sensitive prompts.

title: De-identification and aggregation standards
status_rationale: No de-identification method, aggregate reporting rule or re-identification commitment exists. UNB-GAP-017 calls for defining permissible aggregate reporting.
target_answer: Any de-identified or aggregate output meets a documented standard: minimum cohort sizes and suppression appropriate to small DAF populations, removal of rare grant combinations, and, where statistical release is frequent, formal privacy methods. Echelon publicly commits not to re-identify, contractually binds recipients not to re-identify, and keeps de-identified sets technically separate. Support artifacts and AI evaluation sets are built from synthetic data, not de-identified production data.
current_practice: Unknown; no method or commitment exists.
intended_practice: Define aggregate reporting rules under UNB-GAP-017 before any reporting feature.
customer_statement: Echelon has not defined a de-identification standard. It does not produce de-identified data sets from customer data today.
external_assurance: None. No SOC 2 report, ISO certification, privacy assessment or other independent assurance exists for any Echelon service as of 2026-11-25.
open_questions: Will any product feature (for example charity intelligence or peer giving insights) require cross-sponsor aggregates?
